title: chunk-window-sleuthing-notes
content:
Purpose:
Quick scratchpad for reproducing and isolating a burst-window chunking/backpressure issue seen in hosted API streaming responses. Notes are messy — this is my personal debug log and commands to repro locally + hypotheses to test.

Synopsis (user-facing symptom):
- Intermittent stalls during SSE/text-stream responses where the client sees a long pause (~3-8s) mid-response, then a burst of multiple chunks. Sometimes results in truncated message or client reconnect.
- More frequent on longer responses (>2k tokens) and under moderate concurrency (10-30 rps per instance).

Observed in logs:
- runtime emitter lines show repeated small writes then a long pause:
  [emitter] wrote len=512 backlog=0 (ok)
  [emitter] wrote len=256 backlog=1 (ok)
  ... pause ~5s ...
  [emitter] wrote len=10240 backlog=0 (flush)
- nginx upstream errors sometimes: "upstream prematurely closed connection while reading response header from upstream" (not always)
- client errors: "write EPIPE" or "unexpected EOF while reading chunked body" on some node/python repros

Local repro commands (minimal):
1) Curl SSE stream (single-thread):
   REDWOOD_API_KEY=localkey \n   curl -v -s -H "Accept: text/event-stream" -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_API_KEY" \n     "http://localhost:8080/v1/streams/generate?model=test-streamer&prompt=long-burst"
   - watch timestamps of incoming bytes (use --no-buffer to see streaming behavior)

2) Node fetch client to simulate slow read / backpressure handling:
   (node >=18)
   const res = await fetch(url, { headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${API_KEY}` } });
   const reader = res.body.getReader();
   // read small slices, sleep between reads to simulate slow consumer
   while(true) {
     const { value, done } = await reader.read();
     if(done) break;
     await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 150)); // slow consumer
     process.stdout.write(Buffer.from(value).toString());
   }
   Expect: increased chance of chunk accumulation on server and larger bursts.

3) Python requests (streaming + chunk-size control):
   import requests
   r = requests.get(url, headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {API_KEY}"}, stream=True)
   for chunk in r.iter_content(chunk_size=256):
       time.sleep(0.12)  # slow consumer
       print(len(chunk))

4) Go client (net/http) with explicit small Read buffer to reproduce backpressure:
   // read into 128B buffer, sleep 100ms between reads

Server-side quick configs tried locally: 
- nginx proxy buffering off (proxy_buffering off;) vs on. Observed: proxy_buffering on increases burstiness (buffers chunks and then flushes); turning it off reduces full-message pauses but doesn't eliminate micro-pauses.
- tcp_nodelay=on for runtime worker sockets — small improvement in latency for first bytes but not mid-stream pauses.
- disabled batching (batch_size=1) -> stalls reduced but CPU/tokens per-second cost increased significantly.

Error snippets collected:
- client: "Error: unexpected EOF while reading chunked body"
- node: "FetchError: network error at node: write EPIPE"
- runtime: "conn X: sendto failed: EAGAIN (socket not writable)" followed by large write later that succeeds.

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Upstream buffering + proxy interaction: nginx/k8s ingress buffer semantics + TLS record coalescing cause server flushes to be combined, producing long apparent pauses. Evidence: toggling proxy_buffering changes pause profile.
2) Server-side write path hitting socket backpressure (EPOLLIN/EPOLLOUT transitions) and code doesn't re-schedule writes optimally — writes retried only on request completion rather than on EPOLLOUT events. Log shows EAGAIN then later large write.
3) Continuous batching interactions: runtime waits to assemble batch or KV cache warmup before emitting large chunks; under certain prompt/sequence distributions small early tokens are emitted, then server stalls while waiting for batch/compilation, producing big flush.
4) Client read strategy: some language SDKs read in larger chunks or yield to event loop differently, making behavior worse. Node fetch with reader.getReader() vs eventsource polyfills behave differently.
5) Nagle/TCP coalescing + TLS recordization: small writes get cached then sent in bigger TLS records causing perceived pause. TCP_NODELAY mitigates first-byte latency but not pause between mid-stream writes.

Timeline of attempts: 
- 2026-02-18: initial report from logs (CS) showing user reconnects on long streams.
- 2026-02-21: repro locally with curl + slow consumer. Observed bursts.
- 2026-02-25: toggled nginx proxy_buffering -> bursts reduced.
- 2026-03-02: instrumented emitter to log syscall EAGAIN/bytes_written -> found repeated EAGAIN before big write.
- 2026-03-09: tried disabling continuous batching -> lower incidence but throughput dropped.

Quick repro procedure to hand to SRE/QA:
1) Start local runtime (make dev-runner) with logging level debug for emitter and socket layer.
2) Start a simple nginx proxy in front with proxy_buffering on and a second instance with proxy_buffering off.
3) Run concurrent clients (wrk or custom Node script) with consumer sleep=100ms and concurrency=8.
4) Compare emitter log traces and tcpdump TLS chunk sizes (wireshark) to see if TLS records are coalesced.

Things to instrument next: 
- Per-connection socket writable events (epoll callback timestamps) in runtime to confirm if we're missing EPOLLOUT and only flushing on timer.
- Measure write syscall sizes and count of EAGAIN per logical message.
- Add a small periodic flush heuristic when there are queued bytes older than X ms (50-100ms) to break large pauses — test impact.
- Add per-client slow-consumer metrics: average send queue length and bytes queued.

Notes / To-do for follow-up: 
- @jonah_kim: can you paste the emitter write loop from PR #987 here? suspect scheduling there.
- Test TLS vs plaintext (terminating at nginx vs runtime) to separate TLS coalescing.
- Try forcing TCP_CORK off / TCP_NODELAY on in runtime (already tried node-level TCP_NODELAY).
- Run ab/wrk with --latency to capture distribution.

Questions to ask on #runtime: 
- Do we have a per-socket backpressure counter metric exposed? If not, add one (bytes_queued per socket).
- Is our epoll/IO thread model single-threaded per worker or multiplexed? (I think single IO thread per worker)

Random notes to self: 
- I saw a case where small 128B writes followed by 5s pause then 10KB write happened; that smells like some flush condition or timer gating.
- Could also be interaction with the KV cache cold-start — compiles can delay emission while the model warms up. Add a flag to emit partial tokens while compilation runs.

Reference links / breadcrumbs: 
- Slack: #runtime thread 'streaming bursts' (link pinned to INFR-4532)
- Linear: INFR-4532 (streaming backpressure, barking at nginx)

Bottom line: likely multifactor: proxy buffering + server write scheduling. Short-term mitigations: disable proxy_buffering for SSE routes and add a soft flush timer in runtime. Long-term: instrument and fix EPOLLOUT scheduling/write retry logic.

Last checked: 2026-03-11 — still repros in staging when proxy_buffering=on and consumer is slow.

-- end of notes (temporary, will clean up once we have a definitive repro and PR)
